p: Her father asked about the black ring around the hatch, and Nadia put his question on the risk register: what if the seal ages faster than its data shows?
Gus from the test cell told her the 2019 seal Wes is famous for catching sat in a bag for two years before Wes put it in himself.
FRO's board voted to bid on a second module for Osprey, a company building a smaller station, with three conditions Amara wrote on the back of her card.
Then Brannock's seal lot for HEARTH failed, thirty one percent against a limit of twenty five, and both flight seals went on hold in Ohio.
Nadia hung a red HOLD tag with her name on the seal fixture, and the risk line went up the week it happened.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He owned up to the 2019 seal.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. His lockout rule put Nadia's name on the tag.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She got her bid on a second module.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model, and drew the seal's burn-down chart.
Ken Mallory. Halo's program manager. He sits across the table at every review.
Pavel Ruzicka. Tamarack's lead. The rack is due in week twenty six.
Gus. Test cell technician since the cargo days.
Chapter eight. Thinner Than It Looks.
Nadia came in Saturday morning to finish the review package and found Wes's truck already in the lot, parked across two spaces, the way people park when they've stopped thinking about parking.

The test cell lights were on. He was on a stool by the valve panel with his reading glasses pushed up on his head, looking at the red tag she'd hung on the seal fixture the afternoon before. He didn't turn around.
I got Merle at home, he said. Brannock's plant manager. I bought my first seals off him when he was still running the press himself.
She waited. Wes had a way of telling a thing in the order it had happened to him.

First he says every lot passed. Then he says they've been tuning the post-cure. The oven time after molding. Orders went up last spring and they shortened it to keep up, a little at a time, and every time somebody signed it off as minor. He rubbed his eyes. He couldn't tell me how many times.

He's finding out. I told him to mold ours the old way, the long cure, like their first lot. He said it's the same rubber. I said humor me. For a second he almost smiled. Week nineteen, no charge. He didn't argue about the money. That tells you something.
Did he put that in writing?
Merle's word's been good since before you were born. He stood, folded the glasses into his shirt pocket, and looked at the tag again. Her name, the lot number, yesterday's date. Tiago's rule?

The preliminary design review, PDR, was Thursday. The critical design review, CDR, was planned three weeks after that, at the end of week twenty one. Most of HEARTH's structure came off Wes's cargo drawings, so detail had run alongside, and Halo's node team couldn't finish its own design until HEARTH's was set. That weekend she'd be in Pueblo. She'd texted her father the date with him still on the line.
The wire on the tag had slipped a little overnight. She left him on the stool with the tag. At the top of the stairs she looked back, and he hadn't moved.
Colleen's Flight Notes: what it really weighs.

That afternoon Colleen had her airplane weighed. A shop at the Erie airport drained the fuel, rolled it onto three platform scales, one under each wheel, and read the numbers off a gray box on a cord while Nadia held the clipboard. The empty weight in the logbook had been worked out on paper for decades. A radio in, a heater out, each change added or subtracted with a pencil. The scales said thirty four pounds more than the paper.
Nobody lies on a weight and balance sheet, Colleen said. They just stop checking it.

Design definition is the process that takes the architecture down to the detail needed to build each element. For every element it sets the design characteristics, the values that matter, such as dimensions, materials, mass and power, using design enablers, the equations, models, drawings and heuristics that work them out. It also plans for the enabling systems the element needs, the fixtures and facilities that make, test and handle it. It produces the design artifacts: drawings, specifications, models and parts lists, each traced to requirements and the architecture, with the reasons for the choices recorded. It decides how each element will be obtained, whether made, bought or reused, and checks any reused design against its new conditions. Once approved, the result is the baseline that implementation builds to.

Here's the card for design definition. Its purpose is to give enough detailed data and information about the system and its elements to realize them, consistent with the architecture. It takes in the architecture, the system requirements allocated to each element, and the interface definitions. It puts out the design characteristics and artifacts, the make, buy or reuse decisions, the needs for enabling systems, traces back to the requirements and, once approved, the design baseline. Implementation builds from those artifacts next. System analysis checks them, verification plans against them, and integration works from the interface definitions.

A few habits mark good design work. Designers keep margin. A bracket sized exactly for its largest expected load has nothing left for what nobody knew, so design margins are part of the characteristics, set on purpose and tracked. Every feature traces to a requirement or a need, and a feature that traces to nothing gets justified and traced, or taken out. Designers ask the people who'll build the part to look at the drawings while the design is still open, because a feature that's hard to make is cheapest to fix on paper. Off the shelf items get judged too: whether they meet the requirements as they are, what it costs to adapt them, and who controls their changes and their end of life. And when a design can't meet what the architecture allocated to it, the finding goes back up, and the allocation or the architecture changes. Design and architecture talk to each other the whole way down.

Requirements flow down a specification tree. The system specification sits at the top. Below it sits a specification for each major element, then for the elements inside those, each one traced to its parent. Design definition works at every level of that tree, and each level's design becomes the next level's requirements. Before the formal reviews, peer reviews and walkthroughs catch the easy mistakes early, so the big reviews can spend their time on the hard ones.

How the exam asks it. Design definition turns architecture into buildable detail: characteristics, enablers, artifacts and rationale, traced to requirements. Its output is the design baseline, and implementation builds from its artifacts.

Colleen did two checks before every trip that mattered. The night before, at her kitchen table, she worked the route, the weather and the weights to see whether the trip made sense at all. At the end of the runway, engine running, she checked that this airplane, today, was ready to go.

Design has two gates like that. A preliminary design review asks whether the preliminary design meets the allocated requirements with acceptable risk, so detailed design can start. On many programs it sets the allocated baseline. A critical design review asks whether the detailed design is complete, meets its requirements with adequate margin, and is ready to build, code and integrate. Passing it usually sets the product baseline, the build to set.

Each review has entry criteria, which say what has to exist before it's worth holding: a data package with evidence, sent ahead so reviewers can read it. Exit criteria say what the review must show to close. Reviews are event driven. They happen when the entry criteria are met, not because a date arrived. Every reviewer's item gets a disposition, accepted or rejected with a reason, an owner and a date. A review can pass, pass with actions, or say not yet, and the last one is a legitimate answer.

Reviews run in a sequence that follows the life cycle. A mission or concept review checks that the problem and the concept are understood before requirements are written. The system requirements review checks that the requirements are complete, agreed and ready to baseline. A system functional or definition review checks the functional architecture. Then come the preliminary and critical design reviews, a test readiness review before each formal test, and near the end, reviews that ask whether the system is ready to ship, to operate, or to fly. Names vary by organization and by domain. What doesn't vary is that each one feeds a decision with evidence, against entry and exit criteria everyone knew ahead of time, and each one is a chance to stop.

How the exam asks it. PDR: preliminary design meets allocated requirements with acceptable risk, ready for detail. CDR: detailed design complete, meets requirements, ready to build; sets the product baseline. Reviews are event driven, in order: concept, system requirements, functional, preliminary design, critical design, test readiness, then readiness to ship or operate.

Colleen redid her numbers with the new weight. Her must from the legal pad, full fuel and two passengers, still held, with nineteen pounds to spare instead of fifty three. I flew the old number for two years, she said. I was fine. I just didn't know by how much.

She looked at the gray box on its cord a while longer. I let a colonel talk me out of a feeling one night, she said. Different story. I'll tell you before your test review. Then she went inside to pay the shop.

Measurement collects and reports data so the project can decide things in time. For the design, the measures that matter most are technical performance measures. A technical performance measure follows one critical parameter, such as mass, power, heat rejection or leak rate, against a planned profile over time, with thresholds that trigger action before the requirement is missed. Mass properties engineering tracks mass, center of gravity and inertia for everything aboard, estimated early and confirmed by weighing. It's an engineering specialty, not one of the quality characteristics on the handbook's current list, but nothing that flies gets far without it. Many programs split mass this way. The current best estimate is what the design weighs now. A growth allowance, sized by maturity, covers what it's expected to gain: small for parts already weighed, more for parts calculated from drawings, most for estimates. Estimate plus growth is the predicted mass, and margin is what's left between that and the allocation. The trend matters as much as today's number.

Each TPM gets a plan of its own: the planned value at each milestone, a tolerance band around that plan, and the threshold where action is required. The plan bends on purpose. Mass is expected to grow as drawings mature, so the planned profile climbs toward the allocation and still leaves margin at the end. Reading a TPM means comparing today's value with the planned profile and watching which way it's moving. A value inside the band but trending toward the threshold is the early warning. A value past the threshold is a decision for control. A program keeps only a handful of TPMs, picked from its riskiest and most critical parameters, because tracking everything means watching nothing.

Project assessment and control is the process that acts on those measures. It takes in the plans, the measures and TPMs, and status from the work, and compares what's happening with what was planned. It puts out assessment reports, decisions on corrective action, and sometimes a request to replan. A TPM that crosses its threshold isn't just a red cell on a chart. It's an input that says control has to act: change the design, move an allocation, or spend margin on purpose and on the record. The technical reviews are where those assessments get formal.

Reporting margin honestly is part of the work. A number can be arithmetically true and still mislead. INCOSE's code of ethics asks its members to be honest and objective in what they report, and the people deciding can only act on what they're shown. The same code asks them to guard the safety and welfare of the people their work affects, and to speak up when a decision puts those at risk.

How the exam asks it. Predicted mass is the current estimate plus growth allowance. Margin is allocation minus predicted. Growth allowance isn't margin. Mass properties is an engineering specialty, not a quality characteristic on the current list. TPMs show trends against a plan, early enough to act, and a TPM past its threshold is a trigger for project control.
The shop's mechanic had written up the radio. A different person, an inspector, had signed it off. He doesn't work for the mechanic, Colleen said. That's the point of him.

Configuration management controls changes to anything baselined. A change request says what and why. Each affected area assesses the impact. A configuration control board approves, rejects or defers it. The change is carried into every document and order it touches, and status accounting records where everything stands. Configuration management takes in the items chosen for control and every request to change them. It puts out the baselines, the decision on each change, status records and audit results, and everyone downstream works from them: implementation builds to the current baseline, verification tests it, and transition ships what the audits say is there.

Changes get sorted by what they touch. One that affects form, fit, function, cost, schedule, or an interface with somebody else goes to the full board, and often to the customer. A minor one, like a typo on a drawing, still goes through change control, on a lighter path. Nothing changes a released document quietly. And a change isn't done when it's approved. It's done when every drawing, model, order and procedure it touches says the same thing, and status accounting shows it.

Two processes look after quality. Quality management works at the organization's level: it sets the quality policy, objectives and system, often built on a standard such as ISO 9001, checks whether they're working, and takes corrective action when they aren't. Quality assurance works inside a project: it evaluates the project's products and processes to make sure the organization's quality procedures are being applied, and records the problems it finds. An audit follows a problem wherever it leads, including into the organization's own paperwork. Corrective action fixes the cause, looks for the same gap elsewhere, and checks later that the fix held.

Here's the card for quality management. Its purpose is to make sure products, services and the organization's processes meet its quality objectives and satisfy its customers. It takes in the organization's strategy, what customers report, and the evaluation reports and problem records that projects send up. It puts out the quality policy and objectives, the quality management system with its procedures, evaluation reports, and corrective actions at the level of the organization. Each project's quality assurance applies those procedures next. Quality assurance's own reports go to project control, and when a cause sits in the organization's own procedures, the finding comes back here to fix.

Quality management usually runs on a cycle: plan, do, check, act. It also watches the cost of quality, which sorts spending into four kinds: preventing defects, checking for them, fixing failures found inside the company, and fixing failures the customer finds. The last kind costs the most and hurts the most. Money spent on the first kind is nearly always the cheapest.

How the exam asks it. Change control: request, impact assessment, board decision, implementation, status accounting. Quality management is organizational; quality assurance is per project. Corrective action targets causes, not symptoms.
Monday of week eighteen the forward hatch's qualification article sat on Tiago's stand in the test cell, ready to go into the chamber. Gus was at the valve panel with his hand nowhere near a valve.

The seal fixture sat beside it, built for a shared pumpdown that wasn't going to happen, its sample seal under the red tag. Tiago's opportunity had depended on a fixture ready by Friday. The fixture had been ready. The seal in it was on hold, so he'd let the opportunity go and put the two tests back the way they'd started.

The seal in the hatch's groove came from Brannock's fourth lot, the one at 22 percent, molded after the cure had started getting shorter. It wasn't the seal HEARTH would fly. The flight seals would come from a lot that didn't exist yet. Behind this test the cell was booked solid with the aft hatch through week thirty.
I can pump it down in ten minutes, Tiago said. Tell me what it'll prove.
Brannock's fourth lot seal sits in the qualification hatch, not one HEARTH will fly. How should the test run?
A. Hold the hatch test until the new lot ships, and run it with a flight seal.
B. Run it as planned, and count it as the seal's qualification test as well.
C. Run it to qualify the hatch only, with the seal deviation written down.
D. Drop the qualification leak test and rely on the flight hatch's acceptance.

Tiago writes the deviation on the procedure's first page before Gus touches a valve: seal from lot four, not representative of flight, so this run qualifies the hatch's structure, latches and groove, not the seal. The seal gets its own fixture run on the new lot in week twenty three, in a slot Tiago makes by moving the aft hatch's setup to a Saturday. By Wednesday night the hatch has held for a full day at a third of its allowed leak rate.

That's the one. When a risk turns into an issue, control works out what the planned work can still prove and adjusts the rest. Running the test for what it can honestly show, recording the deviation, and planning the seal's own qualification keeps the evidence straight and the schedule moving.

Tuesday was the day the review package had to go to Halo, forty eight hours ahead, by the review plan. Two things weren't in it. Halo's node team had promised the aft berthing loads in week seventeen and hadn't sent them, so the aft hatch's ring was still sized on the forward hatch's numbers. And the seal for both hatches was a lot on hold in Ohio.
Amara had the package open on her laptop and the contract schedule open beside it.
Push it a week, Wes said. I don't walk into a review with holes in it. Thursday's in the contract, Amara said. They both looked at Nadia.
The PDR package is due today with no aft loads, and the seal lot's on hold. What's Nadia's move?
A. Send the package today as it stands, and let the review find the gaps.
B. Slip the review until Halo's loads are in and the new seal lot has passed.
C. Check each entry criterion against its evidence, and declare the two gaps.
D. Hold PDR Thursday for the forward end, and give the aft end its own review.

Jun builds the checklist from the review plan: requirements allocated and traced, a preliminary design for every element, interfaces at preliminary revision, margins, risks, a verification approach. Eleven of thirteen have evidence. The other two go on the package's first page with an owner and a date each: Halo's aft loads, and the seal lot. Amara reads the page over Nadia's shoulder, then keeps Thursday.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Reviews are event driven. They're held when the entry criteria are met with evidence, and known gaps are declared up front so reviewers can judge the design with the whole picture.

Wednesday Jun was building the slide for HEARTH's technical measures. The model held fifty two numbers with a requirement behind each one, from cabin noise to the hygiene station's flow rate. Amara wanted one slide.
The hatch was in the chamber, a day into its hold, and its leak rate so far was a third of what it was allowed. It was the first measured number for anything on the slide.
Which ones go on it? he asked. If I pick wrong, it's the one nobody looked at that bites us.
Fifty two numbers have requirements behind them, and Amara wants one slide. What should Nadia tell Jun?
A. Put all fifty two on the slide, each with its requirement and today's value.
B. Track drawings released and tests passed each week as the design's progress.
C. Track mass on its own chart, and check the others at each design review.
D. Pick a few tied to key requirements or risks, each with a planned profile.

Four lines: mass, power, heat rejection and leak rate. Each gets its requirement, the value planned for every review from now to ship, a threshold that triggers action, and today's estimate with its margin. Jun draws mass first, a planned line climbing toward the allocation and today's estimate under it. Margin today is 1,010 kilograms.

Exactly right. A TPM tracks a critical parameter against a planned profile, with thresholds, so a bad trend shows before a requirement is missed. Choose them for the requirements and risks that matter most.

PDR ran all Thursday in the conference room over the lobby. Halo sent its program manager, Ken Mallory, with Helen and a structures reviewer who read every load case before she said a word. Odette sat next to the hazard reports. Halo's aft loads arrived at noon, in the middle of it, and they were higher than the forward hatch's. The aft ring would need more metal.
When the aft hatch came up, the structures reviewer asked for the trade behind it, read the weights and the mass score, and moved on.
By five there were thirty one review items on the whiteboard. Some were typos. One said the aft ring couldn't be detailed until it was resized. Mallory capped his pen. Where does that leave us?
Mid review, the aft loads came in higher than the forward hatch's. What should Nadia recommend for PDR?
A. Disposition every item with Halo, then check the exit criteria one by one.
B. Pass it today, and put all thirty one items on a list to close before CDR.
C. Call PDR passed, with every chart shown and no objections raised.
D. Keep PDR open past today until all thirty one review items are closed.

It runs to half past seven. Each item gets accepted or rejected with a reason, an owner and a date. One blocks detail on the aft ring until Wes resizes it for Halo's loads, by Wednesday. The board reads the exit criteria out one at a time. The design meets its allocated requirements with acceptable risk, so PDR passes with nineteen actions, and the allocated baseline is set.

That's the one. A review closes on its exit criteria. Every item gets a disposition, and the review can pass with actions when none shows the design unfit to go on. The approved design becomes the baseline.
Friday morning FRO's buyer forwarded Nadia a note from Brannock's scheduler. The new lot was set for Monday, long cure, per Wes Harland, by phone. Could someone send that in writing?

The seal's drawing named Brannock's material spec by number. Nothing on it said which cure, and the order said standard. Since last night the drawing was under the board, part of HEARTH's allocated baseline.
Wes read the note at his desk. Merle's good for it, he said. I told you that Saturday.
Wes told Brannock long cure by phone, and the scheduler wants it in writing. How should Nadia answer?
A. Let Brannock mold Monday, and write the change request after to match.
B. Write the change request today, and get the board's decision before Monday.
C. Stop the new lot until the audit finds what went wrong, then decide.
D. Let Wes's call to Merle stand as the direction for Monday's lot.

They write it at Wes's desk: the drawing names the long cure, and Brannock has to tell FRO before changing its process again. Odette, Tiago and the buyer assess it before lunch. The board meets at four and approves it, and the buyer sends the order change at five. Wes signs as the requester, and he signs first.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Configuration management controls changes to baselined items: a written request, an impact assessment by those affected, a board decision, and the change carried into the drawings and the order before the work starts.
Brannock's first findings came Monday of week nineteen. Merle had found the count: four cuts to the post-cure since last spring, each approved inside Brannock as minor, each one judged by itself.

Ines, FRO's quality manager, brought the findings to the HEARTH room on Tuesday. FRO's quality system called for an audit after any nonconformance on flight hardware, and she was the one who scoped it. She was small and precise and had a habit of reading a document's revision letter before its title.
Their oven, Wes said. Their problem. Maybe, Ines said. I wrote FRO's purchase template nine years ago. I'd like somebody who isn't me to tell me if I'm auditing the right end.
Ines is scoping the audit after Brannock's four cure cuts. Where should it look?
A. Drop Brannock from the approved list and audit another seal maker.
B. Ask Brannock for its own root cause report and review it closely.
C. Scope the audit to cover both ends of the order, including FRO's.
D. Scope the audit to Brannock's plant, where the cure was changed.

Ines takes Nadia and FRO's buyer to Ohio on Wednesday. They spend the morning in Brannock's change records and the afternoon on FRO's own purchase order, laid out on Brannock's conference table next to the lot certificates. Brannock's quality manager says it's the first time a customer has brought its own paperwork to an audit. Between the two he walks them through the plant. The post-cure oven is about the size of a garage. Its timer is an old dial, and somebody has penciled four marks on the steel next to it, each one a hair left of the last. Every mark got signed, every one was small, and nobody had ever added them up. Ines copies the four marks into her notebook.

Exactly right. Quality management checks whether the quality system is working, and an audit follows a problem wherever it leads, including into the organization's own processes. A supplier's nonconformance often has a cause on the buyer's side too.
Decision seven. What the order asked.
Thursday Ines put her findings on the HEARTH room screen. Two causes, one at each end of the order.

FRO quality audit, HEARTH hatch seal lot nonconformance, findings. Finding 1, Brannock: post-cure shortened four times since last spring. Each change classed as minor and judged alone. No review of the total. No notice to customers. Finding 2, FRO: purchase order called for Brannock standard compound with a certificate of conformance. It did not require aging to the 15 year design life or notice of process changes. Receiving checked that each certificate read PASS.

So whose is it? Wes asked. I'm not writing a name, Ines said. I'm writing two causes. One of them's my template. She said it the way she read revision letters, first. Now I need the corrective action.
The audit has a finding at Brannock and one at FRO. How should FRO respond to them?
A. Send Brannock a corrective action request and close FRO's finding as minor.
B. Add fifteen year aging and a process change clause to this seal order.
C. Test every seal lot at FRO before acceptance, whatever its certificate says.
D. Fix each cause at its source and check FRO's other open orders for it.

Brannock changes its procedure so cure changes add up, and any change to a customer's material gets that customer's notice. FRO's process owner changes the purchase template: anything with a design life gets aging to that life in the order, and a process change clause. The buyer pulls every open order. Eleven have the same gap. Ines puts a date in week thirty to check the fixes held.
That's the one. Quality management takes corrective action on causes, not symptoms: fix the process at each source, look for the same gap elsewhere, and check later that the fix holds.
Monday of week twenty Tiago asked Tamarack for the rack's mass, so he could ballast the stand-in that would go into HEARTH in week twenty four. The real rack would follow in week twenty seven.
Pavel, Tamarack's account lead, called back within the hour.

Six hundred kilograms. The interface control document, ICD revision B, said 560. The 120 volt power card was most of it, then the rear face plumbing and the Ethernet board, all things FRO had asked for.
I should've sent it when the card went in, Pavel said. I thought somebody would weigh it later.
Tamarack's rack weighs six hundred kilograms, and ICD revision B says 560. What's Nadia's next step?
A. Open an ICD change for the mass and assess its impact across HEARTH.
B. Keep the ICD at 560 and let HEARTH's growth allowance absorb the forty.
C. Put six hundred in the mass roll-up, and fix the ICD at its next revision.
D. Hold Tamarack to the ICD and ask them to take the forty kilograms out.

Nadia opens a change to the ICD that afternoon. The impact sheet is full by Tuesday: mount loads up four percent and still inside the brackets' margin, the center of gravity eleven millimeters aft, and forty kilograms plus growth on the mass roll-up. The board approves revision C on Wednesday, and Pavel signs from Frederick. Tiago ballasts the stand-in to six hundred.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. An interface property such as mass is part of the ICD baseline. Changing it takes a change request, impact assessment on every affected item, a board decision, and the new revision issued and recorded.

Tuesday Jun brought the CDR mass roll-up to Nadia's desk. Every line had a maturity next to it. Measured meant somebody had put it on a scale: the berthing mechanism off its vendor's truck, and a few hundred bought boxes weighed at the dock. Calculated meant it came from a released drawing. Estimated meant somebody's best guess, Tamarack's rack among them now. HEARTH's mass plan gave each a growth allowance, two percent, six and fifteen.

The CDR mass roll-up. The allocation is 15,000 kilograms, not to exceed. Measured mass is 3,000 kilograms with 2 percent growth, calculated is 8,500 at 6 percent, and estimated is 1,800 at 15 percent. For CDR, the margin has to be at least 5 percent of the allocation.

Halo's crew office had sent its stowage list that morning, a scan of a printout with a coffee ring on one corner, and Jun had typed every line into the estimated mass. Clothing, eleven kilos a person. Hygiene kits. Exercise bands. At the bottom somebody had added a line in blue ballpoint, small and neat: photos, 40 g. T. Okonjo.

Commander Okonjo, Jun said. She wrote it in herself. Wes had his elbows on the cubicle wall and a coffee going cold in one hand. I'm chasing kilos all over this module, he said, and she wants forty grams. Nobody asked Jun to delete it. Forty grams was a couple of snapshots and a strip of tape, give or take.
How do I show it? Jun asked.
Every mass line now carries a maturity and a growth allowance. Which view belongs on Jun's CDR chart?
A. Plot predicted mass and margin from SRR on, against the planned profile.
B. Show today's predicted mass and its margin against the CDR floor.
C. Show each subsystem's estimate against its own allocation, row by row.
D. Report mass from the drawings now, and add the rack once it's weighed.

Jun plots it from SRR forward: predicted mass climbing toward the allocation, the margin shrinking under it, and the planned margin stepping down at each review. At CDR the margin is 860 kilograms against a floor of 750. It's dropped at every review, and fastest since PDR.
Exactly right. A TPM shows the current predicted value with its growth allowance, against a planned profile and thresholds, over time. The trend tells you more than any single point.
Wednesday Jun stood at Nadia's desk with his laptop and didn't sit down. Wes had seen the chart.

He says margin is allocation minus today's estimate. Seventeen hundred kilograms, eleven percent. He says growth is his pocket. He's kept one on every module he ever built and never once put it on a customer's chart. Jun scrolled to the slide, where his name sat in the corner. He says eight sixty makes Halo nervous, and a nervous customer asks for mass back.
Both numbers came out of the same spreadsheet. Neither one was false.
The slide was due to Halo by Friday.
Wes counts margin as seventeen hundred kilograms, and Jun's slide says 860. What should Nadia do?
A. Use Wes's number, allocation minus today's estimate, as the margin on the chart.
B. Report 860 with the growth shown as its own line, and walk Wes through it.
C. Show both numbers side by side, and let Halo's reviewers pick one.
D. Report 860 now, and add the trend line at the next review once it settles.

They go to Wes's desk together. Nadia says the growth isn't a pocket, it's what the drawings will weigh once they're metal, and Halo's arm will lift what they weigh. Wes leans back in his chair. First module I ever built, I showed the customer my growth, he says. They took half of it for their own boxes. We came in nineteen kilos over, and I spent a month in the high bay drilling holes in brackets to make weight. Halo's going to weigh it anyway, Nadia says. On a crane, at the launch site. I'd rather they saw it coming. Jun shows him the line. Wes looks at it a while. Structure'll use all of its six, he says. Always does. Jun writes that in the notes under the chart, with Wes's name on it.

That's the one. SE in practice includes reporting status honestly, with uncertainty in view, even when the number is unwelcome. INCOSE's code of ethics asks for honesty and objectivity, and decision makers can only act on what they're shown.
Decision eleven. What it's built with.
Monday of week twenty one the CDR package went to Halo. Four hundred and ten drawings, three hundred and eighty six of them released, the aft ring's resized set among them.
The overhead harness channel Wes had taken through the board in week six was on its own released drawing, brackets and all.
Tiago read the package index standing up and handed it back. The lifting fixture isn't in here. Or the transport cradle, or the leak test fixtures. That's ground support, Wes said. CDR's the module.
Tiago and Wes disagree on what belongs in the CDR package. What should Nadia say?
A. List the enabling items as open actions in the package, for after CDR.
B. Add the enabling items' designs to the CDR package alongside the module.
C. Keep the enabling items out of CDR, and design them once the module's set.
D. Hold CDR on its date, and let the release count of ninety four percent decide.

Tiago's list goes in: the lifting fixture, the transport cradle, the leak test fixtures and the rack's handling dolly. Two are designed, two aren't, and those two get dates. On Thursday Halo's structures reviewer opens the lifting fixture's drawing first, because a lifting fixture is what holds a module in the air.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. The fixtures, cradles and test equipment a module needs are enabling systems, and they have to mature alongside the design they support. A detailed design isn't ready to build if what it's built and lifted with isn't designed.

CDR ran Thursday and Friday. On Friday morning Brannock's routine result on the new lot came in: compression set 15 percent, long cure, a pass. The new lot's fifteen year aging result was due in week twenty eight. Jun's backup compound had passed its own qualification on Wednesday, and a change request to add it to the drawing as an alternate was in the board's queue.

The mass chart said 860 kilograms, a hundred and ten over the floor. Mallory stopped on it. Helen asked what the crew would lose first if it went under, and Wes said stowage, before Nadia could. Nadia thought of the forty grams at the bottom of Halo's list. That was stowage too.
At twenty to six the board had heard everything. Mallory looked at his watch and then at Nadia. Does it pass?
The seal lot passed, and mass is a hundred and ten kilograms over the floor. What should Nadia recommend?
A. Pass it, and ask Halo to raise the mass allocation now for later growth.
B. Pass it on the exit criteria, with every margin clearing its CDR floor.
C. Keep CDR open until the mass margin is back above ten percent.
D. Pass it with actions and put the mass margin on watch with a trigger.

With actions, Nadia says. And mass goes on watch. The board reads the exit criteria aloud. The detailed design is complete and meets its requirements, every margin clears its floor, and every review item has a disposition. CDR passes with fourteen actions at ten past six. The released drawings become the product baseline, under the board from tonight. Jun adds one line to the register: mass on watch, trigger at 750 kilograms, with Wes's name beside it.

Exactly right. CDR closes on its exit criteria: a complete detailed design that meets its requirements with adequate margin, ready to build. Passing sets the build to baseline. A margin that clears its floor by a little still gets watched, with a trigger.
CDR was over. Mallory signed the minutes standing up, with his coat on, because his flight left at eight.
The mass chart in his bag had the growth on its own line underneath, and he'd circled the hundred and ten.

Amara walked Halo's people down to the lobby. The Osprey go or no go was Monday, and she'd want this weekend's numbers. Wes went back to his desk, because the aft ring's drawings still had a week of changes in them.

Her bag was already in the car. She was halfway across the high bay to the side door when Tiago called her over. He had the forward hatch's qualification article off its stand and hanging from the crane on its sling, with a load cell between the hook and the sling. Gus, the test cell technician, kept a hand on the tag line so it wouldn't turn.
It had done its leak test. Before it went to storage, Tiago wanted one more number off it.
First piece we've built ourselves on a scale, he said. Sling's zeroed out.
Jun's roll-up had the hatch assembly, door, frame and ring, at 850 kilograms, calculated from released drawings, with six percent on top for growth. Fifty one kilograms of room.
The display climbed, wavered while the hatch settled, and stopped.
Gus read it off. Nine oh six.

Fifty six over the drawings. Five past its whole allowance, on the first part FRO had made with its own hands. She did the rest standing there. If every calculated part came in like this one, growth would run fifty kilograms past what Jun had allowed, and the margin would come down to 810. Sixty over the floor. Wes had said structure would use all of its six percent. This piece had used all of it, and five kilograms more.
That's still a pass, Tiago said. It was. It was inside everything anyone had promised.
Gus lowered it an inch, took it back up, and didn't ask why. The numbers climbed and wavered and stopped in the same place.
Pueblo was two hours south, and her father would ask how the review went, and she'd tell him it passed. Then she'd tell him the rest.
